Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: This item appears misclassified within the Threat node because it describes an avoidance behaviour rather than a threat appraisal or sense of current danger. Given the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, so threat items should plausibly drive coping responses; this item itself is already a maladaptive strategy and duplicates the behavioural content of the Maladaptive Strategies node. The other Threat items (flashbacks, scanning exits) reflect re-experiencing/current danger more coherently for torture trauma.

vignette: Nalini's eyes still scan the crowded streets of New York City with the same intensity she developed during her time in captivity. As a tailor, she is skilled at noticing every detail, from the intricate stitching on a garment to the subtlest change in a customer's expression. But this hypervigilance has become a double-edged sword – it allows her to craft beautiful clothes, but also makes her constantly feel like she's waiting for the other shoe to drop. It started after she was tortured by her captors, who would often burst into her cell without warning. Even now, Nalini can't shake off the feeling that danger lurks around every corner. She scans exits as soon as she enters any room or building, a habit that has become so automatic she doesn't even realize she's doing it. Her friends and family have grown accustomed to seeing her subtly scope out their surroundings, but they don't understand why – Nalini hasn't been able to bring herself to tell them about the torture. As a result of this constant threat monitoring, Nalini has developed a range of maladaptive strategies to cope with her anxiety. She avoids seeking medical or psychological help, fearing that talking about her experiences will somehow make her more vulnerable. She also steers clear of situations that might trigger strong emotions, like watching movies or reading books that deal with themes of trauma or violence. And although she knows it sounds irrational, Nalini has started to avoid relaxing altogether – to her, feeling calm and at ease means letting her guard down, which feels perilously close to inviting disaster. Nalini's avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on her relationships and daily life. Her husband, Rohan, is worried about the distance that's grown between them, but Nalini can't explain why she's been pulling away. She's also started to avoid social gatherings, preferring to stay in her small tailor shop where she can control the environment. As a result, business has slowed down – customers are intimidated by her constant scanning of the room, and they don't understand why she seems so jumpy all the time. Despite her best efforts to keep everything under control, Nalini's symptoms have been escalating over the past few months. She's started having flashbacks – suddenly feeling or acting as if she's back in captivity, with no warning. These episodes leave her shaken and exhausted, making it even harder for her to face the world outside. It was after one of these flashbacks that Nalini realized she needed help – not just for herself, but for Rohan and their future together. She's hoping that therapy can teach her how to quiet the constant threat monitoring in her mind, and learn to trust her own safety once again.
